questions.title: Are these four groups the right way to sort the 52 legal ideas?
questions.plain: We hold 52 ideas drawn from the section 43 material — connotation, likely to deceive or cause confusion, goods of a particular geographical origin, and 49 more. They currently sit in one flat list. The draft model proposes sorting each one into one of four groups: a ground of refusal (a reason an application can be refused), a legal test (a question the decision maker has to answer), a relevant factor (something that feeds into that answer), or an exception (something that takes a case out of the rule). Those four groups exist in the model and every one of them is empty.
questions.why_you: Deciding that "connotation" is a test rather than a factor is a legal judgement. An agent filling those groups would produce a taxonomy that reads as authoritative and was written by nobody. You said you were willing to make calls like this one; it is the single largest gap in the draft.
questions.if_unanswered: The vocabulary stays a flat list. Search and retrieval later have nothing to generalise over — no way to ask "show me every relevant factor" — and 39 of the 52 also sit outside any hierarchy, so the list is close to unstructured.

questions.title: "Deceptively similar" — a section 43 idea, or a section 44 one?
questions.plain: Two approved records disagree. One of the test questions we measure the system against expects a good answer about confusion to mention "deceptively similar". The vocabulary record for "likely to deceive or cause confusion" lists "deceptively similar" as a term that specifically does *not* mean the same thing — on the reading that it belongs to the section 44 comparison between two traders' marks, not to the section 43 question about what a mark says to the public. Both records were signed off. They cannot both stand as written.
questions.why_you: Which of the two is wrong is a question about trade marks law. An agent resolving it either invents a concept or edits an expert's approved record, and both are out of bounds.
questions.if_unanswered: One approved test question keeps naming a term the vocabulary deliberately excludes. Any measurement that uses that question will report a miss that is not a miss.

questions.title: Approve or reject the first automatic rule: the mixed-authority flag
questions.plain: A rule here is a small, fixed instruction that adds a labelled note to the data — not a model, and not anything that changes over time. This one finds passages that quote the Act and state IP Australia's own practice in the same breath, and flags them. It matters because an answer drawn from such a passage can look like it is quoting the law when it has only read the Manual. It flags five passages out of the 216 in scope, and it does find the main section 43 passage, where the Manual quotes the section in full. (This question originally said 71. That was the number of rows of data the rule writes, not the number of passages it flags — see OQ-0019.) Nothing it produces is trusted today: every flag is stored as "candidate — needs a human".
questions.why_you: The programme requires a person to approve every reasoning template before it is used. Nobody has, so its output stays quarantined however well it works.
questions.if_unanswered: The flags exist and nothing may rely on them. Any later feature that would warn "this passage mixes law and practice" cannot be built on a rule that is still pending.

questions.title: Should a saved question be refused unless it says what it cannot answer?
questions.plain: Each question the system can answer is stored as a small saved query. A rule was introduced: a query is refused unless it carries a line saying what it does *not* establish. The reason is that a query returning a neat table always looks like an answer, even when it measured something narrower than the question asked. One of ours counts which parts of the Manual cite section 43 — which is not the same as which parts would need changing if section 43 changed, though it reads that way. The cost is that writing a query takes longer, and the extra time goes on writing down what it does not prove.
questions.why_you: The rule was an agent's reading of what the project's own standard implies rather than what it says. It should be your call before more queries are written against it.

questions.title: All 52 legal ideas are now sorted — and 30 landed in one group. Is the grouping right?
questions.plain:
You asked for the 52 legal ideas to be sorted into four groups: a reason an application can be refused, a question the decision maker has to answer, something that feeds into that answer, and something that takes a case out of the rule. That is now done — every one of the 52 has a group, with the passages behind it and a written argument you can disagree with. Nobody with trade marks expertise has read any of it.
What came back is lopsided and it may be telling you something. Thirty of the 52 are "something that feeds into that answer". Exactly **one** is "a reason an application can be refused". Seven do not fit any of the four at all — those are the people in the process (examiner, decision maker, Registrar) and the procedures around it (opposition, revoking an acceptance, filing a divisional).
There is an innocent explanation and a real one, and only you and your experts can say which. The innocent one: the vocabulary was built entirely around section 43, so nearly everything in it is part of *that* ground's reasoning rather than another ground standing beside it — the shape is correct and would change on its own as the rest of the Manual comes in. The real one: four groups are not enough, and the seven that fit nowhere are evidence of a missing fifth for roles and procedures.
questions.why_you:
This is a question about how examiners actually think about these ideas, and the answer decides the shape of the whole vocabulary rather than any single row. Nothing in the Manual states which group an idea belongs to — every one of the 52 groupings is a reading, and the machine that made them says so on each record.
It is worth asking now rather than after correction, because a fifth group would change roughly a third of the answers, and correcting 52 rows twice is the kind of thing that stops a review round happening at all.

questions.title: The sheet went from 52 ideas to 130, and 53 of them fit none of your four groups
questions.plain:
You asked for the section 43 barrier's removal to show up in the sorting spreadsheet. It does: it held 52 legal ideas and now holds 130. The 78 new ones come from the rest of the Manual — the grounds in sections 39 to 44 and the machinery under each, what a trade mark is, use and ownership, what happens to an application from examination to renewal, the international system, and the two places examination reaches into legislation that is not the Trade Marks Act. Nobody with trade marks expertise has read any of them, and the spreadsheet says so on every row.
OQ-0023 asked whether your four groups were the right shape when 30 of 52 ideas landed in one of them. The wider set answers half of that question and sharpens the other half. The lopsidedness did even out — the innocent explanation was right, and it was an artefact of a vocabulary built around one ground. What did not go away is the pile that fits nowhere: **53 of the 130 are "none of these"**, against 7 of the first 52.
They are not a random 53. They are the people (applicant, opponent, Registrar, registered owner), the documents (notice of opposition, an endorsement, a disclaimer), the proceedings (opposition, a hearing), the outcomes (acceptance, lapsing, a decision) and the remedies (revoking an acceptance, rectifying the Register). Your four groups describe *reasoning* about a trade mark application. Roughly two fifths of the Manual is about *what happens* to one.
questions.why_you:
This is a question about what the vocabulary is for, and only you can answer it. Four groups that cover reasoning are exactly right if the system is meant to help an examiner reason. They are wrong by about 53 ideas if it is also meant to describe the process an application goes through.
It is worth settling before a review round rather than after. If groups get added, roughly two fifths of the 130 rows change, and asking somebody to correct 130 rows twice is how a review round stops happening.

questions.title: How much of the Manual should the graph carry — and it costs about 30MB to carry all of it
questions.plain:
The knowledge graph holds a copy of the Manual passages it reasons over. It used to hold the ones citing section 43 — 216 of the Manual's 2,460 passages — because that was the boundary. With the boundary gone, something had to replace that rule, and a decision was made without asking you because leaving the graph fenced was not an option.
It now holds every passage that any concept, entity or relationship in this repository actually cites, plus the passages around it on the same page, plus every passage where the source data flagged an ambiguous legislative reference. That is 508 passages today, and it grows on its own as more is written — no rule to re-decide.
The alternative was to carry all 2,460. That is the more obvious answer and it costs about 30MB more in the repository, rewritten every time anything is rebuilt. It was measured rather than guessed.
**Here is what the cheaper answer costs, concretely.** One of the questions the system can already answer is *"if section 43 were amended, which parts of the Manual would need reviewing?"* It used to find all 67 passages that cite the section. It now finds 56 — the other 11 are passages nothing in this repository has said anything about, so they are not in the graph. The question still answers and now says on its face that it is counting held passages rather than all of them.
Worth knowing that it was only ever complete for section 43, and only because the boundary happened to be drawn around exactly those passages. It was incomplete for every other section in the Act and nothing said so.
questions.why_you: It is a cost question, not a correctness one — both answers are honest, and neither excludes anything from scope. Whether 30MB of repository churn is worth "the whole Manual is always there" is your call about the project, not a judgement about trade marks law.

questions.title: The court decisions — what that other repository actually holds
questions.plain: You said the decisions are in scope and pointed at your IP-Decision-Data repository. It was checked. It holds an index of 8,900 Australian intellectual property documents, 7,282 of them court decisions, and the index is the citation and a web address — **not a word of what any court said**. The full text is produced by the same pipeline but is deliberately not stored in the repository; it exists only as a build attachment, which expires. Of the 58 decisions the section 43 material cites, **15 are in that index and 43 are not** — the missing ones are mostly Trade Marks Office delegate decisions and pre-1990 reported cases, which the source corpus does not carry.
questions.why_you: Three things follow and none is an agent's call: whether 15 of 58 is worth building on, where the actual text is to come from and where it may be stored, and whether the missing 43 — the delegate decisions especially — matter enough to go looking for separately. There is also a licensing question about holding decision text at all.
questions.if_unanswered: Nothing is blocked. "Which cases interpret this test" stays answerable and "what did the court hold" stays unanswerable, which is recorded and which a prohibition already stops the system pretending otherwise about.

questions.title: Your one-hop boundary rule, and where the Manual does not cooperate
questions.plain: Your rule — one hop, and the hop lands on the specific chunk rather than its parent section — is implemented and reported. It works: twelve parent provisions stay out of scope purely because of your second sentence. But it does not do what you expected for section 41. You wrote that section 43 would refer to a number of specific chunks within section 41; in fact the Manual writes "section 41" bare in 32 of the section 43 passages, as well as citing 41(3) and 41(4). A bare citation names the whole section, so the whole of section 41 comes into scope and your second sentence never engages. Twenty-two provisions behave this way, including sections 42 and 44.
questions.why_you: The rule met a corpus that cites more loosely than the rule assumes. Which way to resolve that is a scope judgement about how much neighbouring law the pilot carries, and it changes how much material everything downstream has to account for.
questions.if_unanswered: The boundary stays as computed — wider than you probably intended, with the whole of sections 41, 42 and 44 inside it. Nothing breaks; the pilot is simply larger than the rule reads as describing.

questions.title: Should a rule about what an examiner must do be recorded like any other relationship?
questions.plain: You asked whether a glossary captures the relationship between an examiner and a registrar, and said to adopt a Must/May predicate if it does not. It does not — a glossary holds one entry per term, and "an examiner must consult a team leader before accepting on doubt" is a relationship between two roles with a force attached, which no arrangement of definitions holds. So the predicate is adopted, and it turned out to exist already: every approved relationship can carry must, may or should. What was missing was the ability to make a relationship be *about* a role at all, and that is now possible. Nothing has been written into it.
questions.why_you: Whether examiner conduct genuinely belongs in the same structure as "connotation must arise from the mark itself" is a judgement about the domain, not about the software. Recording a duty as a relationship makes it answerable by the same machinery as everything else, which is the argument for; it also flattens a rule about people into a shape built for rules about legal ideas, which is the argument against.
questions.if_unanswered: The shape exists and stays empty, which is the honest state. The expert's note about the Registrar's actual bar for the presumption of registrability stays where it is, in the file it arrived in, and is not in the knowledge base.

questions.title: Where exactly does section 43 stop?
questions.plain: The pilot area is section 43. The boundary is not drawn: which parts of the Manual count as in, which neighbouring provisions come with it, whether geographical indications are the centre of the topic or a corner of it, and whether questions about how the law stood at an earlier date are in scope. A draft boundary exists for an expert to correct, with the numbers behind each choice.
questions.why_you: Drawing it needs someone who knows what an examiner actually reaches for.
questions.if_unanswered: Every remaining piece of expert content stays unscoped. It does not block the review round, which was designed not to depend on it.

answered.how: You typed the answer into issue #12 by hand, outside the form.

questions.title: The office's actual bar for the presumption of registrability
questions.plain: An expert's note said the draft examples capture the presumption of registrability and the idea of doubt, but not the bar the office actually applies: it is not enough for the individual examiner to doubt, and an examiner is expected to consult a team leader and the section 43 specialists before accepting on that basis. That is a rule about how examiners behave, and no kind of record we hold is shaped to store it.
questions.why_you: Whether it becomes a new kind of record, an entry in the scope document, or something else is a call for the expert and you together.
questions.if_unanswered: A materially important piece of practice sits in a note and not in the knowledge base.

answered.how: You typed the answer into issue #12 by hand, outside the form.

questions.title: Nine role terms with no definitions — Registrar, Delegate, Examiner and more
questions.plain: The same expert note said the draft vocabulary was drawn from one Part of the Manual, which gives a narrow view of who does what. Nine terms were named as needing high-level definitions — Registrar, Delegate, Examiner, Decision Maker, Office Practice, Subject Matter Expert, Oppositions, Grounds for Rejection, Adverse Report — "and there are likely more". There is a trap underneath: the rule that selects passages picks ones that cite section 43, and a term's definition is usually not in a passage that cites anything.
questions.why_you: Whether the fix is an exception to that rule, a separate definitions pass, or importing an existing glossary is an expert and owner call.
questions.if_unanswered: The vocabulary keeps describing the test and not the people applying it.

questions.title: May a bare "section 15(1)" be read as the Trade Marks Act?
questions.plain: The expert rejected two draft prohibitions on a principle worth recording: that inferring a bare "section 15(1)" means the Trade Marks Act is acceptable given what this tool is for, and that the tool should be able to say when a passage is quoting legislation. That sits against the upstream position, which refuses to resolve an ambiguous reference at all. The two are not quite the same claim — upstream's ambiguity is about which of several instruments is meant — but a session must not quietly assume either reading.
questions.why_you: Where the line sits between a safe inference and an invented one is a judgement about the corpus, not about code.
questions.if_unanswered: Citation resolution in a later stage has no agreed rule, and one kind of prohibited use rests on a single record.
